title: Pulmonary Embolism: A Comprehensive Clinical Blueprint
summary: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is a life-threatening occlusion of the pulmonary arterial system, most commonly secondary to Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). Rapid identification via risk stratification (Wells Score) and definitive imaging (CTPA) is vital for reducing the high mortality associated with right ventricular failure.

data.title: Pulmonary Embolism: A Comprehensive Clinical Blueprint
data.summary: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is a life-threatening occlusion of the pulmonary arterial system, most commonly secondary to Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is the most serious clinical manifestation of Venous Thromboembolism (VTE). It occurs when a thrombus (or occasionally fat, air, or amniotic fluid) migrates from the systemic venous circulation to the pulmonary arterial tree. This leads to a ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch, increased pulmonary vascular resistance, and potential right ventricular (RV) failure.

branches: Hypercoagulability (Factor V Leiden, Cancer, OCP, Protein C/S Deficiency)

rows: Alternative diagnosis less likely than PE

sections.title: Clinical Presentation & Physical Signs
content: Sudden onset dyspnea (85% of cases)
Pleuritic chest pain (Inflammation of the pleura)
Tachycardia (HR > 100 bpm) and Tachypnea (RR > 20/min)
Cough and Hemoptysis (indicative of pulmonary infarction)
Syncope (signifies massive PE and reduced cardiac output)
Accentuated P2 (Loud second heart sound component)
Distended jugular veins (JVD)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: Step 1: Clinical Assessment & Wells Score calculation
Step 2: D-Dimer test (if low clinical probability) to rule out
Step 3: CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) - Gold Standard
Step 4: V/Q Scan (if CTPA is contraindicated, e.g., renal failure)
Step 5: Lower limb Doppler USG if DVT is suspected
Step 6: Bedside Echo to assess RV strain in unstable patients

content.explanation: S-wave in Lead I, Q-wave in Lead III, and Inverted T-wave in Lead III. Note: Sinus Tachycardia is actually the most common finding; S1Q3T3 is specific for RV strain but rare.

sections.title: Ocular Connection: Fat Embolism Syndrome
content: Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES) can present as a subtype of PE
Triad: Respiratory distress, petechial rash, and confusion
Ocular Findings: Purtscher-like Retinopathy
Cotton-wool spots and Purtscher flecken (ischaemic retinal whitening)
Caused by occlusion of precapillary arterioles by fat globules

sections.title: Acute Management Protocol
content: 1. Oxygen Supplementation (Maintain SpO2 >90%)
2. Fluid Resuscitation (Cautious, to avoid RV over-distention)
3. Anticoagulation: UFH (bolus then infusion) or LMWH (Enoxaparin 1mg/kg BID)
4. Thrombolysis (Alteplase 100mg over 2h) for Massive PE
5. IVC Filter: Only if anticoagulation is contraindicated or fails

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Hemodynamic Instability
content: Systolic Blood Pressure < 90 mmHg for > 15 minutes
Refractory hypoxia despite 100% FiO2
Altered Mental Status / Impending Doom
New-onset Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB) on ECG
Evidence of Right Ventricular Dilation on Echo (RV > LV size)

sections.title: Long-Term Anticoagulation Options
content: DOACs (First line): Apixaban, Rivaroxaban (no bridging needed)
Warfarin (Vitamin K Antagonist): Requires Heparin bridge (INR 2.0-3.0)
Duration: 3 months for provoked PE (surgery/trauma)
Duration: Extended/Indefinite for unprovoked or recurrent VTE
Special consideration: LMWH is preferred in pregnancy and active cancer

sections.title: Landmark Studies in PE
sections.content: PEITHO Trial: Demonstrated that while thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE prevents hemodynamic collapse, it significantly increases the risk of major hemorrhage and stroke. MOPETT Trial: Suggested that 'Safe Dose' (half-dose) thrombolysis may be effective with fewer bleeding complications for submassive PE.

sections.title: Surgical & Interventional Techniques
content: Surgical Embolectomy: Indicated for massive PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated
Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis (CDT): Lower dose of Alteplase delivered via ultrasound-assisted catheter
Mechanical Thrombectomy: Fragmenting and aspirating the clot via percutaneous route
ECMO: Veno-arterial (VA) ECMO for circulatory support in extreme shock

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: A normal Chest X-ray in a setting of severe hypoxia is a strong hint for PE (Westermark sign and Hampton’s hump are classic but rare).
D-dimer has high negative predictive value but low specificity; it is useless in post-operative or pregnant patients.

In the Ophthalmic Perioperative setting: If a patient on anticoagulants requires urgent surgery (e.g., ruptured globe), discuss reversing with Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC) vs. Heparin bridging.
Tachycardia is often the only sign in the early stages—never ignore it in a post-surgical patient.
